hashing-python-functions::0.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::0.snippetHtml: title: Working with Python where-functions published: 2025-06-16 updated: 2025-06-16 description: Hashing the unhashable abstract: | It is impossible in general to verify the equivalence of functions in terms of their input-output behaviour, or semantics. Many programming languages, including Python, don't evaluate functions' equivalence in terms of their code structure, or syntax, either. Nor does Python compute hashes of functions based on their structure, but merely their memory address. So it doesn't make sense to represent a mapping from some tree node-accessors to some respective node data, using a dict where the node-accessors (that is, where-functions) are keys. But what if I very wisely insist I must build such a dict anyway? However misguided, it turns out solving this problem helps us with a more practical one: serialising hyperparameters for training runs, when those hyperparameters happen to be where-functions.

hashing-python-functions::1.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::1.snippetHtml:
For the past two years, I've developed my machine learning projects with JAX and Equinox. The basis of JAX's power is how flexibly we can compose our computation graphs by writing in a functional paradigm, using transformations like grad, vmap, and jit. But the substance of its power is PyTrees, or the ability to transform over arbitrary types of tree-structured inputs in a unified way.

To be clear: "a PyTree" is code for "some nested composition of nodes, which JAX knows how to treat like any other tree because it's been told how to flatten and unflatten the nodes".

hashing-python-functions::3.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::3.snippetHtml: Where-functions are just functions which access one or more nodes from an input PyTree: they return a different PyTree, composed of one or more nodes from the input.

hashing-python-functions::4.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::4.snippetHtml: One use case is to edit the nodes of a PyTree out-of-place. Suppose we have an instance of some data type:

hashing-python-functions::5.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::5.snippetHtml:
import jax
import equinox as eqx
from equinox import Module

class Foo(Module):
    bar: dict[str, int]
...
hashing-python-functions::5.codeText:
```python
import jax
import equinox as eqx
from equinox import Module

class Foo(Module):
    bar: dict[str, int]
    baz: tuple[float, float]

    def __call__(self, x: jax.Array):
        # If `Foo` were part of a model, we could transform `x` here, 
        # using `self.bar` and `self.baz` as parameters.
        ...

tree = Foo(
    dict(a=1, b=2),
    (3.14, 2.718)
)
```

hashing-python-functions::6.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::6.snippetHtml: An Equinox Module is a type of Python dataclass, which JAX can manipulate as a PyTree.

hashing-python-functions::7.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::7.snippetHtml: A where-function lets us specify the nodes whose values will be replaced:

hashing-python-functions::8.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::8.snippetHtml:
where_nodes_to_update = lambda tree: (tree.bar['a'], tree.baz)

# Update some parts of the tree
updated_tree = eqx.tree_at(
    where_nodes_to_update,
    tree,
...
hashing-python-functions::8.codeText:
```python
where_nodes_to_update = lambda tree: (tree.bar['a'], tree.baz)

# Update some parts of the tree
updated_tree = eqx.tree_at(
    where_nodes_to_update,
    tree,
    (5, (6.28, 1.618)),
) 

updated_tree 
>> Foo(bar={'a': 5, 'b': 2}, baz=(6.28, 1.618))
```

hashing-python-functions::9.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::9.snippetHtml: Similarly, suppose we are given a PyTree of default model states (i.e. arrays), and we'd like to initialize some its leaves using custom arrays. For each leaf we want to initialize, we could pair its where-function with an appropriate array value. But maybe we don't know beforehand exactly which leaves we'll want to initialize, so we'd like a general tool that can perform the initialization for us in any case:

hashing-python-functions::10.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::10.snippetHtml:
from collections.abc import Callable
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree

def replace_nodes(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[tuple[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, node_value in spec:
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, node_value)
...
hashing-python-functions::10.codeText:
```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree

def replace_nodes(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[tuple[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, node_value in spec:
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, node_value)
    return tree
```

hashing-python-functions::11.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::11.snippetHtml: This works, so long as the structure of the node values matches the structure of their respective where-function's return value. However, of course some of our where-functions might pick out trees containing redundant leaves from tree, and in that case we'll end up pointlessly replacing the same leaf more than once. Perhaps it is better to assume in this case that our where-functions will specify individual, unique leaves (or at least, trees of non-intersecting subsets of leaves). So, suppose instead we use the function:

hashing-python-functions::12.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::12.snippetHtml:
def replace_leaves(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[dict[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, leaf_value in spec.items():
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, leaf_value)
    return tree

hashing-python-functions::13.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::13.snippetHtml: Now we can specify a mapping between where-functions that pick out unique leaves, and the arrays we should replace those leaves with:

hashing-python-functions::14.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::14.snippetHtml:
# Assume these have already been assigned
default_state: PyTree[Array]  
some_part_init_data: Array
some_other_init_data: Array

# Construct the mapping from parts of the state PyTree, to the data to initialize them with
...
hashing-python-functions::14.codeText:
```python
# Assume these have already been assigned
default_state: PyTree[Array]  
some_part_init_data: Array
some_other_init_data: Array

# Construct the mapping from parts of the state PyTree, to the data to initialize them with
init_state_spec: dict[Callable, Array] = {
    (lambda state: state.some_substate.part): some_part_init_data,
    (lambda state: state.some_other_substate.other_part): some_other_init_data,
} 

# Update the default state with the custom init states
initial_state = replace_nodes(default_state, init_state_spec)
```

hashing-python-functions::15.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::15.snippetHtml: This does work, but all is not what it seems. We'll encounter some strange behaviour if we assume that init_state_spec treats its where-function leaves as unique, because they pick out unique leaves.

hashing-python-functions::16.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::16.snippetHtml: For example, if in some other context we want to determine which data will be used to initialize states.some_substate.part, we might try to access it like so:

hashing-python-functions::18.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::18.snippetHtml: But this doesn't return some_part_init_data! It actually raises a KeyError.

hashing-python-functions::19.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::19.snippetHtml: Likewise, if we already have some init_state_spec and want to update it to use some different data for part of the state, we might try this:

hashing-python-functions::21.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::21.snippetHtml: But this actually adds a new entry to the mapping, rather than replacing the old one.

hashing-python-functions::22.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::22.snippetHtml: What is responsible for this weirdness? Well, Python accesses and assigns dict entries based on the uniqueness of a key's hash... and this doesn't work like you might think, or like I once naively hoped, when the key happens to be a function.

hashing-python-functions::24.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::24.snippetHtml: Any Python object that can be hashed[^1] can be used as a key in a dict. While a Python function is hashable, its hash is based on its object identity, which in CPython (i.e. for almost all Python users) is just its memory address. For example, all of the following expressions evaluate to False:

hashing-python-functions::25.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::25.snippetHtml:
# Explicitly compare by object identity
id(lambda x: x) == id(lambda x: x)  
(lambda x: x) is (lambda x: x)

# Implicitly compare by object identity
(lambda x: x) == (lambda x: x)
...
hashing-python-functions::25.codeText:
```python
# Explicitly compare by object identity
id(lambda x: x) == id(lambda x: x)  
(lambda x: x) is (lambda x: x)

# Implicitly compare by object identity
(lambda x: x) == (lambda x: x)

# Explicitly compare by hash
hash(lambda x: x) == hash(lambda x: x)
```

hashing-python-functions::26.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::26.snippetHtml: Since these will evaluate False for any function, and since where-functions are of course "any function", this example is also False:

hashing-python-functions::27.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::27.codeText:
```python
hash(lambda model: model.some_layer) == hash(lambda model: model.some_layer)
```

hashing-python-functions::28.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::28.snippetHtml: At first this might seem kind of weird. Not only is lambda model: model.some_layer obviously identical to lambda model: model.some_layer in how it's written (i.e. its structure, or syntax), but the two are also obviously identical in how we should expect them to behave (i.e. their meaning, or semantics). Actually, in the case of a where-function, syntax and semantics are pretty closely aligned in general: once we know its syntax then we can be pretty certain about what it is going to return, and vice versa, since it's just performing some simple accesses of parts of a data structure.

hashing-python-functions::29.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::29.snippetHtml: If functions were hashed in terms of either syntax or semantics, then our where-functions' uniqueness would be determined in the way we want. Seems pretty useful! So why wouldn't Python evaluate hashes or equivalence, in terms of either syntax or semantics?

hashing-python-functions::30.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::30.snippetHtml: Semantics? That's easy. And by "easy", of course I mean impossible: it's a well-known mathematical fact that there's no general method by which we can test whether any two functions will always behave the same way, for all inputs. So if programming language designers want tools like hash and == operators to be general-purpose, and useful for comparing any two functions their users might write, then those tools can't be based on semantics.

hashing-python-functions::31.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::31.snippetHtml: We could also try to evaluate equivalence in terms of syntax, which is the structure of the function's code. This is at least possible, when we have access to the code. But it could be kind of expensive (ref?). Maybe it's enough most of the time to know that two functions aren't literally identical in memory. Anyway, that's what Python assumes!

hashing-python-functions::32.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::32.snippetHtml: Since dict uses hash to determine the uniqueness of keys, and the hash of a where-function is not determined by what it picks out, dict cannot see our where-functions the way we see them.

hashing-python-functions::34.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::34.snippetHtml: Once upon a time I decided that I really wanted to be able to use where-functions as dict keys. I realized that where-functions do not hash in terms of the part(s) of a PyTree they access, and decided to make a custom type of dict that did not directly treat where-functions as keys, but instead converted them to an intermediate value which would hash on my terms. And for that, I needed a function that takes a where-function as input, and returns a hashable representation of the where-function's syntax as output.

hashing-python-functions::35.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::35.snippetHtml: Essentially, we want a function that So I searched for a function where_func_to_str that would convert a where-function to a string. I expected it to behave like so:

hashing-python-functions::36.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::36.codeText:
```python
where_func_to_str(lambda state: state.layer2)
>> "layer2"

where_func_to_str(lambda s: s.some_substate.layer1)
>> "some_substate.layer1"
```

hashing-python-functions::37.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::37.snippetHtml: And maybe I could also get it to work for slightly more complex cases:

hashing-python-functions::39.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::39.snippetHtml: I hadn't yet imagined how I would handle all possible where-functions. For example, this would be no good:

hashing-python-functions::41.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::41.snippetHtml: That's because lists, including ["layer2", "layer3"], aren't hashable. They can't be used as keys! Nor can dicts or sets

hashing-python-functions::42.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::42.snippetHtml: • But why not just "[layer2, layer3]" inside a single string?

hashing-python-functions::43.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::43.snippetHtml: But why not just "[layer2, layer3]" inside a single string?

hashing-python-functions::44.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::44.snippetHtml: 1. Notice that the name of the bound variable ("state", "s", whatever) does not matter here. What is important is that given some PyTree, whatever its name, we are accessing some part(s) of it, whose names are given.

hashing-python-functions::45.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::45.snippetHtml: Notice that the name of the bound variable ("state", "s", whatever) does not matter here. What is important is that given some PyTree, whatever its name, we are accessing some part(s) of it, whose names are given.

hashing-python-functions::46.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::46.snippetHtml: 1. What about other kinds of access, e.g. lambda state: state.layer2['foo']?

hashing-python-functions::47.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::47.snippetHtml: What about other kinds of access, e.g. lambda state: state.layer2['foo']?

hashing-python-functions::48.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::48.snippetHtml: 1. What about where-functions that return non-hashable types? For example, lambda state: [state.layer2]?

hashing-python-functions::49.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::49.snippetHtml: What about where-functions that return non-hashable types? For example, lambda state: [state.layer2]?

hashing-python-functions::50.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::50.snippetHtml: Tuples are also hashable, so ("layer2", "layer3") is fine as a dict key. However, assuming we do find a where_func_to_str that works like we want, we'll need to make sure our where-functions return PyTrees which are hashable when their leaves are replaced with strings.

hashing-python-functions::51.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::51.snippetHtml: On my quest for a where-based dict, I made three attempts to write a where_func_to_str. But let's start with an example that will not work.

hashing-python-functions::53.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::53.snippetHtml: That is, a string literal containing the code as it appears in the source file. This is the most direct comparison we can make. It's pretty cheap, since we just need to compare the strings character-by-character until there is a single mismatch. However, it's pretty naive, and hardly useful. Note that none of the following functions will test as equivalent if we compare them literally, though their syntactic differences are trivial:

hashing-python-functions::54.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::54.snippetHtml:
def func(x):
    return x + 1

def func_with_comment(x):
    return x + 1  # ooowee

...

hashing-python-functions::55.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::55.snippetHtml: Maybe works, but I didn't think to try it: abstract syntax tree

hashing-python-functions::56.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::56.snippetHtml: An Abstract syntax tree (AST) is a data structure specifically intended to represent the syntax of a program. Python's ast implementation would say that all of the functions in the previous example have equivalent ASTs. However it, like most AST implementations includes the naming of bound variable as part of the syntax. So for example:

hashing-python-functions::57.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::57.snippetHtml:
def compare_ast(*code: str):
    tree_dumps = [ast.dump(ast.parse(s)) for s in code]
    return len(set(tree_dumps)) == 1

compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda x: (x)")  # True
compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda y: y")  # False; the only difference is a bound variable name
...
hashing-python-functions::57.codeText:
```python
def compare_ast(*code: str):
    tree_dumps = [ast.dump(ast.parse(s)) for s in code]
    return len(set(tree_dumps)) == 1

compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda x: (x)")  # True
compare_ast("lambda x: x", "lambda y: y")  # False; the only difference is a bound variable name
```

hashing-python-functions::58.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::58.snippetHtml: There are good reasons why we'd want to preserve bound variable names in ASTs, but when testing for the syntactic equivalence of functions, or when trying to evaluate the hash of a we generally admit alpha equivalence, and normalizing our ASTs to an alpha-equivalent form can require a little work when dealing with arbitrarily complex functions with nested scopes of bound variables.

hashing-python-functions::59.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::59.snippetHtml: In any case, generating ASTs may be kind of expensive, especially if we don't know beforehand how complex the things we want to compare will be, as is the case when a language designer is implementing a general operator like ==.

hashing-python-functions::61.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::61.snippetHtml: Once Python has parsed the literal source code, it encodes the program as a sequence of lower-level instructions for the interpreter to run the program. Therefore, bytecode is language-dependent; bytecode in Python looks different than bytecode for a different interpreted language. Parsing does involve some semantic interpretation, and unlike an AST, bytecode is not mainly intended as a representation of syntax. But we can imagine the syntax of the resulting bytecode as a practically abstracted form of the syntax of our source code.

hashing-python-functions::62.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::62.snippetHtml: So in some cases, it might make sense to compare the bytecode of two functions, to test for some kind of equivalence.

hashing-python-functions::63.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::63.snippetHtml:
from collections.abc import Callable
import dis


def get_where_str(where_func: Callable) -> str:
    """
...
hashing-python-functions::63.codeText:
```python
from collections.abc import Callable
import dis


def get_where_str(where_func: Callable) -> str:
    """
    Returns a string representation of the (nested) attributes accessed by a function.

    Only works for functions that take a single argument, and return that argument,
    or a single (nested) attribute accessed from the argument.
    """
    bytecode = dis.Bytecode(where_func)
    return ".".join(
        instr.argrepr for instr in bytecode 
        if instr.opname == "LOAD_ATTR"
    )
```

hashing-python-functions::64.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::64.snippetHtml: But this is inefficient, inflexible, and really not best practice in Python.

hashing-python-functions::65.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::65.snippetHtml: It only works for a single attribute access. To make it work for arbitrarily complex subtrees would be annoying.

hashing-python-functions::67.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::67.snippetHtml: My second attempt used the PyTree facilities from JAX+Equinox to use the where-function to modify the respective nodes of the PyTree, then figure out what their paths are, and return those. The paths are certainly one-to-one with their string representations.

hashing-python-functions::68.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::68.snippetHtml: While this method is in some ways more flexible than using bytecode, it was even slower. Also it required access to the tree we will be using the where-function on (or more technically, one that shares at least all the same node paths accessed by the where-function).

hashing-python-functions::69.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::69.snippetHtml:
from collections.abc import Callable

import equinox as eqx
import jax.tree as jt
from jaxtyping import PyTree

...

hashing-python-functions::71.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::71.snippetHtml: The third solution, and the best one I've found so far, is based on passing an instance of special class to the where-function.

hashing-python-functions::72.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::72.snippetHtml: By defining the attribute-access and item-access behaviour for this class, we can easily construct a tree-of-strings representation of the structure of the where-function's return value. This is the most flexible method, and also by far the fastest.

hashing-python-functions::73.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::73.snippetHtml:
from collections.abc import Callable

import jax.tree as jt
from jaxtyping import PyTree


...

hashing-python-functions::74.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::74.snippetHtml: This still isn't super efficient -- about 10 µs per call, for the data I'm working with -- but I only need to do a small number of these operations every training iteration, so for my purposes it was okay.

hashing-python-functions::75.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::75.snippetHtml: Now that we have a decent where_func_to_str, we can construct the custom dict that effectively uses where-functions as keys. This is interesting, but since it no longer has much to do with the where-functions themselves, I've

hashing-python-functions::77.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::77.snippetHtml:
Another common use case for a where-function is to define the parts of a model which will be trained:

Our model objects are typically PyTrees whose nodes are of type eqx.Module. In this case, our where-function assumes that our model possesses whichever nodes it refers to.

hashing-python-functions::79.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::79.snippetHtml: Notice that where_train has the flavour of a hyperparameter: on different training runs or phases, we might want to train different parts of the model. So we might want to encode where_train in our hyperparameter data, similarly to how we would encode the number of training iterations, or the learning rate.

hashing-python-functions::80.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::80.snippetHtml: Of course, it can be kind of inefficient to try to encode functions as data (e.g. an AST). And if we want our encoding to reflect the effect (i.e. semantics) of the function rather than simply the way it was coded, there is no general solution. But since we're working with where-functions in particular, we can just use where_func_to_str to convert them to an equivalent representation which is easily serialisable:

hashing-python-functions::82.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::82.snippetHtml: Of course, we'll probably want to deserialise this representation and convert it back into a where-function, like when loading hyperparameters from disk to start a training run. But the reverse transformation is not too difficult:

hashing-python-functions::83.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::83.snippetHtml:
from collections.abc import Callable
from operator import attrgetter

from jaxtyping import PyTree


...
hashing-python-functions::83.codeText:
```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from operator import attrgetter

from jaxtyping import PyTree


def attr_str_tree_to_where_func(tree: PyTree[str, 'T']) -> Callable[[[PyTree], PyTree[Any, 'T']]:
    """Reverse transformation to `where_func_to_attr_str_tree`.

    Takes a PyTree of strings describing attribute accesses, and returns a function
    that returns a PyTree of attributes.
    """
    getters = jt.map(lambda s: attrgetter(s), tree)

    def where_func(obj):
        return jt.map(lambda g: g(obj), getters)

    return where_func
```

hashing-python-functions::84.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::84.snippetHtml: NOTE: Though this is still missing the reverse getitem logic, mainly because I've only ever serialised functions that make attribute accesses.

hashing-python-functions::86.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::86.snippetHtml: I found this pretty interesting, and I learned a lot.

hashing-python-functions::87.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::87.snippetHtml: I am not a computer scientist, nor super knowledgeable about algorithms, so if you've read this far and you think I'm missing something obvious or that I've taken the wrong approach, I trust you to mention it!

hashing-python-functions::89.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::89.snippetHtml: We'll start by defining the general case of a dict that which transforms its keys before trying to hash them.

hashing-python-functions::92.codeText:
```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar

import equinox as eqx
import jax.tree as jt
from jax.tree_util import register_pytree_node_class
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree


T = TypeVar('T')


def _where_to_str(where: Callable) -> str:
    """Return a single string representing a where-function."""
    terms = where_func_to_attr_str_tree(where)
    if isinstance(terms, str):
        where_str = terms
    else:
        where_str = ", ".join(jt.leaves(terms))
    return where_str

@register_pytree_node_class
class WhereDict(AbstractTransformedOrderedDict[str, Callable[[PyTree], Any], T]):
    """An `OrderedDict` that allows use of where-functions as keys.

    In particular, keys can be callables (functions/lambdas) that take a single argument,
    and return a PyTree of leaves, as visited by attribute/item accesses.

    Functions are parsed to strings, which can be used interchangeably as keys. 
    For example, the following return the same value when `init_spec` is a `WhereDict`:

    > init_spec[lambda state: state.mechanics.effector]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector']  

    Finally, a `tuple[Callable, str]` may also be provided as a key, for cases where
    different unique entries must be included for the same callable. For example,
    the following are equivalent:

    > init_spec[(lambda state: state.mechanics.effector, "first")]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector#first']

    Note that the hash symbol `#` is used as a delimiter in the string representation.

    ??? Note "Performance"
        For typical initialization mappings (1-10 items) construction is on the order
        of 50x slower than `OrderedDict`. Access is about 2-20x slower, depending
        whether indexed by string or by callable.

        However, we only need to do a single construction and a single access of
        init_spec per batch/evaluation, so performance shouldn't matter too much in
        practice: the added overhead is <50 us/batch, and a batch normally takes
        at least 20,000 us to train.
    """

    def _key_transform(self, key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:
        return self.key_transform(key)

    @staticmethod
    def key_transform(key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:

        if isinstance(key, str):
            pass
        elif isinstance(key, Callable):
            where_str = _where_to_str(key)
            return where_str
        elif isinstance(key, tuple):
            if not isinstance(key[0], Callable) or not isinstance(key[1], str):
                raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                                 "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
            where_str = _where_to_str(key[0])
            return '#'.join([where_str, key[1]])
        else:
            raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                             "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
        return key

    def __repr__(self):
        return eqx.tree_pformat(self)
```

sidenotes-demo::2.title: Sidenotes and Margin Notes Demo
sidenotes-demo::2.snippetHtml:
This post demonstrates how to use both Tufte-style sidenotes[^1] and margin notes in your blog posts.

Margin notes are unnumbered and appear without any superscript in the main text.

sidenotes-demo::3.title: Sidenotes and Margin Notes Demo
sidenotes-demo::3.snippetHtml:
Sidenotes use standard footnote syntax and are numbered sequentially[^2], while margin notes use a different syntax and appear without numbers.

They're perfect for brief clarifications that don't need explicit referencing. You can even include bold text, italic text, inline code, and markdown links within them!

sidenotes-demo::5.title: Sidenotes and Margin Notes Demo
sidenotes-demo::5.snippetHtml: Edward Tufte's approach to sidenotes[^3] prioritizes keeping supplementary information close to the relevant text, rather than forcing readers to jump to the bottom of the page.

sidenotes-demo::6.title: Sidenotes and Margin Notes Demo
sidenotes-demo::6.snippetHtml: The implementation follows the principles outlined in Tufte CSS[^4], providing an elegant reading experience that doesn't interrupt the flow of the main text.
